extracted.intended_audience: Researchers asked to serve as peer reviewers for PLOS Computational Biology (computational biology journal reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for researchers performing peer review of original research manuscripts submitted to PLOS Computational Biology, covering whether to accept invitations, how to assess manuscripts, what to include in reports, conflicts of interest, confidentiality, and journal processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept invitation only with knowledge, time, and objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept an invitation only if you have the knowledge, time and objectivity necessary to provide an unbiased assessment of the research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the links in the invitation email or the Reviewer Main Menu in Editorial Manager to accept/decline. If you accept, you also give permission to publish your review under a Creative Commons Attribution CC BY license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permission to publish review (CC BY)
rubrics_metrics.description: By agreeing to complete a review, you give permission to publish your review under a Creative Commons Attribution CC BY license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you choose to sign your review your name will appear alongside your comments in the editorial decision letter and, if the authors publish peer review history, alongside the published article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review model and anonymity options
rubrics_metrics.description: PLOS Computational Biology practices single-anonymized peer review by default, but offers options for reviewers to sign reviews and for authors to publish peer review histories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In single-anonymized review you know the authors' names but your name will not be shared. You may choose to sign your name; if authors publish peer review history your name will appear if you signed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portable reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews may accompany manuscripts if authors transfer to another PLOS journal, and you may be asked to re-review by another PLOS editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers for any PLOS journal should be willing to have their reviews considered by editors of another PLOS journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaring competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: A competing interest is anything that interferes with or could be perceived as potentially interfering with a thorough and objective assessment of a manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common examples: recent/current collaboration with any authors; direct competition or history of scientific conflict with authors; opportunity to profit financially from the work. Do not accept if you have a competing interest or cannot give an objective assessment. If unsure, contact the journal office. If asked to review despite a competing interest, declare it when you submit your review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crediting collaborators (co-reviewing disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you had help completing the review you must share your collaborator’s name with the journal when you submit the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enter the name in the question labeled 'Has this review been co-authored with a colleague?' or email the journal. Do not include your collaborator’s name in the text of the review itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep manuscripts and correspondence confidential and do not share information about submissions with anyone else unless previously agreed with the editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make use of any material or take advantage of any information gained through the peer review process. Read the PLOS Confidentiality Policy for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing a manuscript previously reviewed elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: If you reviewed the article at another journal, treat the manuscript as a new submission unless instructed otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscript may have been revised and PLOS’ criteria may differ. When submitting your review, tell the editor if you reviewed a previous version at another journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeframe for review completion
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to complete your review within 14 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need more time, email the journal as soon as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer credit (ORCID and Publons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Link PLOS reviewer account to ORCID or Publons to receive credit for completed reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up syncing to have reviewer activity automatically posted to ORCID; this confirms completion but will not publish the content of the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility for publication — overall criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to ethical conduct and scientific validity, research should fulfill each of the PLOS Computational Biology criteria for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these criteria alongside editorial and publishing policies when assessing manuscripts; see separate entries for each criterion below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: The work should be original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the paper's claims are novel and whether prior published articles weaken claims of originality. Ask reviewers to identify relevant prior work that challenges originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: The work should be innovative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the submission uses novel concepts, approaches, or methods that advance the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: High importance to researchers in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: The research should be of high importance to researchers in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the significance and potential impact of the main claims for the discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant biological and/or methodological insight
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper should provide significant biological and/or methodological insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the results yield important new understanding or methods that the field will use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: The study should employ rigorous methodology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate study design, statistical analysis, computational methods, controls, and whether methods are appropriate and robust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial evidence for conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be substantial evidence supporting the manuscript’s conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the data and analyses fully support the claims; if not, specify what other evidence is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify main claims and their significance
rubrics_metrics.description: State the main claims of the paper and assess how significant they are for the discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the claims; explain their importance and how they advance understanding or methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess novelty and cite weakening literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claims are novel and, if not, identify published articles that weaken the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide references and clear explanation of how prior work affects novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize claims in previous literature and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether claims are properly placed in context of previous literature and whether the authors have treated the literature fairly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note omissions or biased citation practices and request corrections or additions where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and analyses must support claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the data and analyses fully support the manuscript’s claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence is insufficient, specify what additional analyses or data are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advise on additional work and feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend whether additional work would improve the paper and estimate how much improvement and how difficult the work would be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between essential revisions versus optional enhancements and be realistic about scope and feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protocols and algorithms as supporting information
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend publishing detailed protocols and algorithms as supporting information online when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If methods warrant such treatment (e.g., detailed computational protocols or randomized controlled trial protocols), suggest providing them; check for important deviations from provided protocols and ask for explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original data deposition and accession numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Original data should be deposited in appropriate repositories with accession/version numbers provided for genes, proteins, mutants, diseases, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify presence of repository links and accession numbers; request deposition if missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-generated code availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Author-generated code that underpins the findings should be made publicly available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether code is deposited in an appropriate public repository and whether it is sufficient to reproduce analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformance to relevant reporting guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies should conform to relevant guidelines such as CONSORT, MIAME, QUORUM, STROBE, and the Fort Lauderdale agreement where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask authors to document compliance and provide checklists if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological detail for reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological details should be sufficient to allow experiments and analyses to be reproduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request clarifications or additional methodological detail when reproducibility is impeded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Any software created by the authors should be freely available where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess licensing and accessibility; request availability statements or repositories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript organization and clarity for non-specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: The manuscript should be well organized and written clearly enough to be accessible to non-specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out organizational problems, unclear passages, or jargon-heavy sections and suggest improvements for broader accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and explanation of standardized nomenclature and abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper should use standardized scientific nomenclature and abbreviations, and explain non-standard terms at first usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request definitions or changes where nomenclature is inconsistent or unexplained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct remarks that help strengthen the paper to authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Although confidential comments to editors are respected, any remarks that might help strengthen the paper should be directed to the authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve confidential comments for matters that legitimately must remain private to the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to re-review revised manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are often asked to evaluate revised manuscripts and authors’ responses; reviewers should try to make themselves available for re-review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to follow up on revisions and answer editors' questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing reviewers’ reports — non-editing policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial Board members should not edit or delete reviewer reports, and must notify PLOS staff before sending a decision letter if they have concerns about suitability of a reviewer’s comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PLOS staff will not change reviewer comments intended for authors except when language is inappropriate for professional communication or when comments contain confidential information or would incur major risk if conveyed. PLOS will not edit/remove reviews for decisions already delivered to authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor decision process
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors make the final decision on publication based on reviewers’ comments, the journal’s criteria for publication, and their own assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should be aware that decisions are not strictly majority-rule; editors balance reviews, author responses, and other material not available to reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling conflicting reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviewers disagree fundamentally, editors may share all reviews with reviewers and request additional comments to help reach a decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions are not necessarily by majority; editors may seek extra input or adjudication when experts disagree.
